question: Metal and ceramic coatings have been investigated for zirconium-alloy fuel cladding. Comparative testing found that several candidate coatings performed adequately under either normal subcritical-water conditions or accident-relevant high-temperature steam, but not under both. Elemental Cr coatings provided comparatively strong protection in both environments; however, elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion caused premature coating failure. Any solution must therefore preserve protection across both service regimes while maintaining coating integrity, limiting interfacial element transport, and remaining stable in extreme nuclear environments. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve the durability of an elemental Cr coating on zirconium-alloy cladding? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, states the applicable temperature, exposure-time, and environmental boundaries, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment that separately evaluates oxidation behavior, coating integrity, and interfacial element transport.
